lessons.title: Why Valuing a Startup Is Nothing Like Valuing a Listed Stock

children.text: Search any Nifty 50 company on screener.in and within seconds you have its market cap, P/E ratio, ROCE, ten years of audited financials and a share price that updated a moment ago. Now try to value a two-year-old startup. You get a pitch deck, eighteen months of revenue, a spreadsheet projecting ₹100 crore of sales by 2031 and a founder who is very sure. The tools you use for listed stocks were built for the first situation. This lesson shows why they break in the second, and what a startup valuation really is.

body.text: A listed stock's price is discovered by thousands of buyers and sellers every trading day. A startup's valuation is negotiated by a handful of people once every year or two. One is a measurement. The other is a deal term.

children.text: How a Listed Stock Gets Its Value

When you buy a stock on NSE through Zerodha, the price is set by the order book. Every buyer and seller brings their own view, and the last traded price is where those views met. Multiply that price by the shares outstanding and you have the market capitalisation.

body.caption: For a listed company, value is observed, not negotiated

children.text: Analysts then check whether that price makes sense using tools that depend on three things listed companies have plenty of: profits, history and disclosure.
P/E ratio.
Price divided by earnings per share. Needs positive, reasonably stable earnings.
EV/EBITDA.
Enterprise value divided by operating profit. Needs a business that already generates operating profit.
Discounted cash flow (DCF).
Forecast future cash flows and discount them to today. Needs a track record to forecast from.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Open any listed company and notice how much verified data you get for free. Then ask how much of it exists for a startup you are evaluating.

body.title: Show me why a startup DCF is fragile

children.text: Suppose you believe a startup will be worth ₹50 crore in five years. What is that worth today? It depends entirely on the discount rate, and for early-stage startups nobody agrees on one. Venture investors often use rates of 40% to 60% or more to reflect the chance of failure.

content.caption: Present value of a ₹50 crore outcome in five years

children.text: One assumption changes the answer by almost three times, and that is before you question whether ₹50 crore is realistic at all. A DCF can still be a useful thinking tool for a startup. It is just not a reliable price.
Startups Are Bets on Rare Outcomes

A listed company is usually valued on what it is likely to earn. A startup is valued on what it might become if things go very right. Picture a seed-stage startup with three possible outcomes over seven years.

body.title: Three possible outcomes for one seed-stage startup (illustrative)

body.caption: Probability-weighted value of the three outcomes

children.text: The expected value is ₹56 crore, but notice where it comes from. ₹50 crore of the ₹56 crore comes from the 10% breakout case. The most likely single outcome, with a 60% chance, is zero. That is why startup valuations can look absurd next to current revenue: investors are pricing the small chance of a very large result, not the typical one.

body.text: For an individual angel, this changes how you should think about any single valuation. If most of a startup's value sits in a 10% tail, one cheque is closer to a lottery ticket than to a stock purchase. Only a portfolio of many startups gives the averages a chance to work.

body.title: Weigh the outcomes
body.prompt: A startup has a 70% chance of shutting down, a 25% chance of being acquired for ₹40 crore and a 5% chance of reaching ₹800 crore. What is its expected value, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: (0.70 × 0) + (0.25 × 40) + (0.05 × 800) = 0 + 10 + 40 = ₹50 crore. Four-fifths of the expected value comes from a 5% chance. The most likely outcome is still zero.

children.text: So What Is a Startup Valuation, Really?
A startup valuation is the price at which one investor agreed to buy new shares in one round, extended to the whole company. It is shaped less by spreadsheets and more by the following forces.
How much money the company needs.
Founders raise enough to reach the next milestone, usually 18 to 24 months of runway.
How much dilution founders will accept.
A round often sells somewhere between 10% and 25% of the company. Divide the cheque by that percentage and the valuation follows.
Competition among investors.
Two term sheets push the price up. None pushes it down, or kills the round.
The funding climate.
The same startup could command a far higher valuation in the 2021 boom than in the 2022 to 2023 funding winter.
Comparable rounds.
What similar startups at similar stages raised at recently.
Traction and team.
Revenue growth, retention, and founders who have built and sold something before.

body.label: The core valuation shortcut
body.context: An investor putting in ₹2 crore for 20% implies a post-money valuation of ₹10 crore. Lesson 2.2 unpacks pre-money, post-money and price per share properly.

children.text: Private Valuations Move Without Anyone Trading

Because there is no market price, a startup's value between rounds is just an estimate, and different investors can hold very different estimates of the same company. Swiggy shows how far those estimates can swing.

body.title: Swiggy: one company, very different marks

events.title: Peak private round
events.description: Swiggy raises about $700 million in a round led by Invesco, at a reported valuation of around $10.7 billion.

events.title: Investor markdowns
events.description: During the funding winter, Invesco reportedly cuts the value of its Swiggy holding more than once, at one point implying a valuation of roughly $5.5 billion. No new round took place. The company simply got marked down.

events.title: Listed on NSE and BSE
events.description: Swiggy goes public with an IPO priced at ₹390 per share, valuing it at roughly $11 billion. For the first time, the market sets the price every day.

body.text: Markdowns cut both ways. PharmEasy's parent was valued at about $5.6 billion in 2021, and in 2023 it raised money through a rights issue at a valuation reported to be roughly 90% lower. Any investor who had treated the 2021 figure as "what my shares are worth" learned that a private valuation is only as good as the next investor willing to pay it.

body.text: The headline number is not even the value of every share. A round valuation is usually set by investors buying CCPS with liquidation preference. Equity shares without those rights are worth less, which is why an independent fair market value report for tax or ESOP purposes can come in well below the latest round price. Lesson 2.4 covers the Indian valuation rules.

body.title: The right tool
body.question: A Pune SaaS startup has ₹6 crore of annual revenue, an operating loss of ₹9 crore and 14 months of cash left. Why is a P/E ratio useless for valuing it?
options: P/E only works for companies listed on NSE
The company has negative earnings, so P/E has no meaningful value
SaaS companies are always valued on EV/EBITDA
Its revenue is too small to calculate earnings per share
body.explanation: P/E divides price by earnings. With a ₹9 crore loss, there are no positive earnings to divide by, so the ratio tells you nothing. EV/EBITDA fails for the same reason. Early-stage valuation has to rely on other methods, covered in Lesson 2.3.

body.title: How the price is set
body.textWithBlank: A listed stock's price is discovered in the market. A startup's valuation is set by ___ between founders and investors in a funding round.
body.explanation: A startup valuation is a deal term agreed between a small number of parties, shaped by how much money is needed, investor competition and the funding climate.

body.title: The stale valuation
body.scenario: In 2026, a relationship manager offers you shares in a Gurugram consumer startup through a secondary sale. "It was valued at ₹800 crore in its last round, so ₹20 lakh gets you a clean 0.025%." You find that the last round closed in late 2021, revenue has been roughly flat since, and the company has not raised money since then.
body.prompt: Is ₹800 crore a fair basis for your price? What would you check before investing?
body.modelAnswer:
No. ₹800 crore was a price agreed in the 2021 boom, and nothing since then has confirmed it. Flat revenue and no new round for over four years both suggest the company would struggle to raise at that valuation today.

Checks before investing:
1. When was the last priced round, who led it, and on what instrument? A 2021 CCPS price with liquidation preference is not the right price for equity shares in 2026.
2. Have any existing investors marked the company down in their fund reports?
3. What is the current runway, and does the company need to raise again soon, possibly in a down round?
4. How have listed or recently funded comparable companies been valued since 2021?
5. What share class are you buying, and does the seller have the right to transfer it under the Articles and shareholders' agreement?
6. Is there an independent recent valuation report?

If the answers are weak, the ₹800 crore headline should be treated as a ceiling from another era, not a starting point.

cards.definition: Last traded share price multiplied by shares outstanding. Observed, not negotiated.
The price per share agreed in a funding round, applied to the whole company.
The probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes.
The rate used to convert future value into value today. Higher risk means a higher rate and a lower present value.
An investor reducing the value at which it carries a private holding, without any new round taking place.
A period when investors deploy less capital and valuations fall, as in India in 2022 and 2023.

points: Listed stock prices are discovered by the market every day. Startup valuations are negotiated once per round.
P/E, EV/EBITDA and DCF depend on profits, history and disclosure, which early-stage startups lack.
A startup DCF swings wildly with the discount rate, so it is a thinking tool, not a price.
Startup valuations price a small chance of a very large outcome. The most likely single outcome is often zero.
Round valuations are driven by capital needed, dilution accepted, investor competition, the funding climate and comparable deals.
Private valuations can be marked up or down without any trade, as Swiggy and PharmEasy show. Always ask when and how a valuation was set.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation on any company named. Valuation figures for Swiggy and PharmEasy are based on public reports and are approximate. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
